description: The QUIC control plane's shared vectors (plan docs/plans/2026-11-14-quic-data-plane.md). Swift (`mac/Tests/QuicControlVectorTests.swift`, `QuicCapsVectorTests.swift`) and Kotlin (`QuicControlVectorTest.kt`, `QuicCapsVectorTest.kt`) run the same cases against their own code; the Rust core checks the ALPN constant (`mobile/native-src/quic-core/tests/vectors.rs`). Sections: `constants`, `actions` (the q.* actions inside a `cmd`), `channels` (the stream type header), `stat` (the `caps` field), `handshake` (who may send what, when), `gate` (who may open a session, what the controls show), `transport` (which path a file takes: QUIC stream, the WebSocket path, wait for the LAN, or too large), `file_stream` (the bytes of the QUIC file stream).

constants.description: Values both sides must share byte for byte. `alpn` is the TLS ALPN protocol id of the data plane (a version change bumps the suffix); `max_action_bytes` is the largest action string (UTF-8 bytes) either side parses; `accept_timeout_ms` is how long the side that asked waits for the other side's accept (and how long the phone waits for its user). `ws_file_limit_bytes` is the largest file the WebSocket `file` path carries (1 GiB): Swift `FileFrame.maxTransferBytes` and Kotlin `FileFrame.MAX_TRANSFER_BYTES` must both equal it, and the `transport` section's thresholds are built on it. The `file_*` values are the QUIC file stream's limits (`file_header_max_bytes` the largest header message, `file_name_max_bytes` and `file_mime_max_bytes` the field limits, `file_first_byte_timeout_ms` how long a receiver waits for the first byte of a bidirectional stream before it ignores the stream, `file_size_max` the largest `size`).

actions.description: The q.* actions that open and close a QUIC session, as the JSON string inside a `cmd`. `kind: parse` — `text` (a `{PAD}` marker is replaced by `pad`: `{char, to_bytes}` makes the whole text exactly that many UTF-8 bytes, `{char, count}` repeats the character) parsed with `allow_echo` (default false); `expect.result` is `action` (and `encoded`, the canonical form of the parsed action: keys in alphabetical order, no whitespace, session id lower case), `unknown` (a JSON object whose `a` is missing or not one of the five: ignored quietly) or `invalid` with a short `code`. `kind: encode` — an action object and the exact canonical string it must encode to; every encoded string must also parse back to itself.

channels.description: The first varint of every data stream names its channel: 1 file (bidi), 2 screen (uni), 3 camera (uni). `kind: header` — the bytes (`hex`) a sender writes for a channel (the shortest varint) and its stream `direction`. `kind: parse` — the first varint of `hex` read by a receiver: `channel` + `consumed` bytes, `unknown` (any other value, with the `value`), or `needMoreBytes`. Every QUIC varint length (1, 2, 4, 8 bytes) is read; a longer-than-necessary encoding is accepted (RFC 9000 allows it); only the first varint is consumed.

stat.description: `caps` is an array of capability names. Absent (or not an array) means 'no information': the receiver keeps what it has, so a battery or proximity stat never clobbers it. An array SETS the known capabilities (unknown names and non-string items are ignored; an empty array means 'supports none'). Today the only known name is `q1`; names are exact (case-sensitive). When the peer goes offline the set is cleared; until a stat with `caps` arrives, the peer is treated as not supporting QUIC. `kind: parse` — a decoded stat object and the update `QuicCaps.parse` must give (`absent` or `set` with `caps`). `kind: sequence` — steps applied in order to a fresh PeerCaps (`stat` with a stat object, `offline`), and the set expected after each step. `kind: available` — `quicAvailable` is true only on the LAN-direct link AND with `q1` known. `kind: advertise` — what a side writes into its own stat: [`q1`] when it supports QUIC, nothing otherwise.

handshake.description: The handshake rules of one session (`side` mac|phone, `asker` = this side sent the q.req, `start_ms`, optional `timeout_ms` for the accept wait, default 60000). `initial` is the phase at the start; each step is `send` (this side wants to send `action`), `receive` (the peer's `action` arrives) or `tick` (the clock reaches `at_ms`), with `expect` = `{applied: phase}` or `{ignored: code}` (for send/receive) or `{phase}` (tick), and an optional `then` = the phase the session must be in afterwards. A phase is `{name, deadline_ms?}` (awaitingAccept, awaitingUser, awaitingOffer, mayOffer, offered) or `{name: closed, close: ended|timedOut|rejected, reason?}`. The offer is always the Mac's; with the phone as the asker there is no accept step; an offer before the accept is ignored; after `closed` everything is ignored.

gate.description: Who may open a QUIC session, and what the controls show. `incoming`: a peer's q.req arrives; the answer is `busy` (a session is already active; checked FIRST so a running session is never disturbed), `relay` (the link is not the LAN-direct one), `unsupported` (this side does not serve that kind) or `proceed`. `visible`: whether QUIC controls are shown at all: only on the LAN-direct link AND when the peer announced `q1` (the same rule as `stat.available`). `outgoing`: this side wants to ask: `hidden` (the peer never announced `q1`: nothing to ask), then the same order busy, relay, unsupported, proceed. Both the Mac (`QuicGate`, Swift) and the phone (`QuicGate`, Kotlin) run every case.

transport.description: Which path one file takes (plan stage 2.1, Faz 2). `kind: choose` — `link` (`lan` = the LAN-direct link is the active one, `relay`), `caps` (the capability names the peer announced in its stat), `size` (bytes; `null` = not known yet), `clipboard` (a clipboard image, which is always one frame) and `expect`: `quic` (a QUIC stream per file, no size limit), `ws` (the existing WebSocket `file` path, limit `ws_file_limit_bytes`), `waitForLan` (too big for the WebSocket path, and the peer can do QUIC once the phone and the Mac are on the same LAN again) or `tooLarge` (too big and no way to send it: the peer cannot do QUIC, or the link is LAN-direct without `q1`). Rules in order, first match: a clipboard image is `ws` whatever its size; the LAN link with `q1` is `quic` (also when the size is unknown); an unknown size is `ws`; a size up to and including the limit is `ws`; above it, the relay with `q1` is `waitForLan`, everything else `tooLarge`. The section is the full cross product (2 links x 3 capability sets x 6 sizes x 2 kinds = 72), so no combination can be skipped silently; the exact edge is the limit itself (`ws`) and the limit plus one byte.

file_stream.description: The QUIC file stream (plan stage 2.2, Faz 2): one bidirectional stream per file. The sender writes the file channel varint `0x01` (the shortest form; the two-byte form `4001` is accepted) and a header message; the receiver answers `{"have":N}` (the bytes it already holds, 0 <= N <= size) or a refusal `{"err":"...","ok":false}`; the sender writes exactly `size - have` raw bytes and closes its side; the receiver answers `{"ok":true}` only after the file is in its final place, or a refusal. Every message is `u16 BE length || JSON`. What a SENDER writes is canonical JSON: keys in alphabetical order, no whitespace, `\"` `\\` and control characters escaped (`\b \f \n \r \t` in short form, others as `\u00xx` lower case), everything else raw UTF-8; what a RECEIVER reads is any JSON with the same meaning. Header (`header_encode`, `header_parse`): `id` (8 lower-case hex), `mime` (1-255 bytes), `mtime` (integer >= 0), `name` (1-200 UTF-8 bytes), `size` (integer 0..2^53-1), optional `dir` (a string); other fields are ignored. A number counts as an integer only when it is written as one: `1.5`, `5.0`, `1e3`, `"5"` and `true` are not. The message is at most 4096 bytes. `header_parse` feeds the bytes the way a stream delivers them: `expect.result` is `header` (the fields and how many bytes it used; later bytes belong to the body), `needMore`, or `invalid` with `code`: `not-file` (the first varint is another channel: not ours, nothing is answered), `bad-header` (anything wrong with the structure or limits) or `bad-id` (the structure is fine but `id` is not 8 lower-case hex; checked last). Splitting the same bytes at any position must give the same result. `have_parse` (the sender reads the first answer, `size` = the file size): `have` (0 <= N <= size), `err` (a refusal; an unknown or missing code is `unknown`) or `invalid`. `result_parse` (the last answer): `ok`, `err` or `invalid`. `have_encode`, `result_encode`: the exact bytes. Error codes: `space`, `busy`, `bad-id`, `write`, `too-many`, `bad-header`, `size`. `body_length` (size - have, or null when have is outside 0..size) and `finish_verdict` (the sender closed its side after `received` bytes while `expected` were due: `ok` when equal, otherwise `size`). Lone surrogate escapes and duplicate keys are not pinned.
